# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

Adam's stationary calibration field averages a nonlinear readout of joint first- and second-moment memories. Linear momentum preserves $h$, whereas @eq-covariance-decomposition shows why centring the ordinary innovation need not centre Adam's readout. The field depends on the joint stationary memory law and hence potentially on temporal dependence, beyond the invariant one-time innovation marginal. No model-specific Metropolis--Hastings root displacement has been established here.

For a frozen Markov driver with a unique invariant probability and a finite second innovation moment, the fixed-gain memories admit a finite-dimensional Markov augmentation with a unique invariant law. The integral in @eq-stationary-adam-integral represents the stationary Adam field under this law. Under the additional driver coupling and spatial regularity assumptions of @thm-wasserstein-lifting, the augmented transition laws also converge at a geometric rate in Wasserstein distance. This forward argument does not require time reversal, and it supplies the quantitative contraction used in the invariant-measure perturbation and frozen Poisson results of [@RudolfSchweizer2018; @Hofstadler2026].

The Markovian iterated-function-system results of [@Fuh2021] provide a useful comparison. Their analysis allows contraction conditions formulated through random Lipschitz coefficients and stationary averages, rather than a uniform metric contraction at every memory update. It therefore motivates investigating which of the geometric coupling and regularity assumptions in the present framework can be weakened while retaining the quantitative bounds required for Wasserstein perturbation and Poisson control. We do not claim that the rates or conclusions of [@Fuh2021] imply the Wasserstein Dobrushin estimates used here.

Parameter regularity can likewise be reduced to properties of the driver and its forcing. In particular, @eq-augmented-operator-perturbation separates the change of the driving transition from the change of the memory update, and @cor-invariant-parameter transfers this estimate to the augmented invariant law. These calculations do not impose weighted total-variation ergodicity on the augmented process. Contractive deterministic memories can converge in Wasserstein while their transition laws remain mutually singular at every finite time.

For bounded innovations, the square-root second-moment coordinate gives a natural metric in which both the memory update and Adam's normalised readout are Lipschitz. This is relevant to acceptance-rate calibration, where the innovation is bounded. More general unbounded innovations may require different metrics or additional regularity of the readout.

The parameter-dependent Poisson statement in @prp-poisson-parameter uses an additional Lipschitz-operator perturbation bound. The weaker weighted pointwise kernel estimate, although sufficient for the invariant-law result, does not establish this bound automatically. Closing that distinction and then controlling the adaptive martingale and summation-by-parts remainders are the remaining steps towards ODE tracking of $F$. Convergence to a root of $h$, or even to a single equilibrium of $F$, remains a separate question. The present results establish the stationary covariance identity and a quantitative framework for studying its behaviour under controlled Markov noise, without identifying a particular adaptive-MCMC equilibrium.
